technical.technical:
The five image models on this surface, in the detail the box on the page leaves out.

SD 1.5 generates the picture by denoising in a compressed latent space, and the prompt goes through one frozen CLIP encoder (Rombach et al. 2022, "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models", CVPR 2022, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2112.10752). SDXL is built on that construction, with OpenCLIP ViT-bigG beside CLIP ViT-L. Podell et al. (2023, "SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis", ICLR 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.01952) give the two denoisers as 860M and 2.6B parameters. Esser et al. (2024, "Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis", ICML 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.03206) then replace the U-Net with a transformer whose blocks carry text and image through the same attention mechanism with weights of their own, trained on rectified flow; SD 3.5 Large has 8.1B parameters in that backbone, beside the two CLIP encoders and a T5-XXL of 4.7B. Black Forest Labs gives the Flux 2 Dev model that runs here as 32B parameters, with a 24B Mistral as its text encoder. For Gemini 3 Pro, Google names the architecture only by reference to its text model and describes the training data by category; the parameter count stays unpublished.

Every parameter count above is the count of the PICTURE-MAKING network alone: 860M and 2.6B are U-Nets, 8.1B is the MMDiT backbone, 32B is the FLUX.2 rectified-flow transformer. The text encoders are counted separately. Read otherwise, 8.1B against 32B compares a backbone with a backbone plus its 24B text encoder.

What varies alongside the model, read off devserver/schemas/configs/output/: SD 1.5 runs 512 x 512, 25 steps, CFG 7.5, sampler euler_ancestral, through ComfyUI. SDXL 1024 x 1024, 30 steps, CFG 7, euler_ancestral, ComfyUI. SD 3.5 Large 1024 x 1024, 25 steps, CFG 5.5, euler, Diffusers. Flux 2 Dev 1024 x 1024, 20 steps, CFG 1, euler, ComfyUI. Gemini 3 Pro Image is reached as a cloud service and none of these settings apply to it; its config carries no seed field. All four local configs carry an empty negative prompt, so no column suppresses anything the others keep.

The seed: the same number goes to every column whose config has a seed field, and that serves reproducibility. It leaves the starting noise different all the same. The sampler of each column draws its noise through its own generator - ComfyUI's KSampler against a Diffusers torch.Generator - and into a latent of its own shape: 64 x 64 x 4 at 512 x 512, against 128 x 128 x 4 and 128 x 128 x 16 at 1024 x 1024.

One run per model. A difference between two single pictures is not yet a measured difference between two models: the surface is a demonstration, and the model is one of several things that differ between two columns.

Ho et al. (2020) is NO source for the point about the seed, and it was taken out of the references on the page on 2026-09-07. Its "nearly zero mutual information" holds between the endpoint of the FORWARD process and the training datum, and two of the five columns run euler, a deterministic sampler under which the starting noise fixes the picture completely.
technical.reading: Modelle sind nicht neutral — jedes hat eigene Vorlieben (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md). Die Reihe mit der festen Startzahl hält alles außer dem Modell fest, sodass sie zeigt, was jedes Modell aus demselben Satz macht. Die fertigen Sätze über dem Eingabefeld sind nach dem Eigenschaften-Katalog der zentralen Presets ausgewählt (UCD-118, Plan Rev. 3); jeder benennt eine beobachtbare Eigenschaft: „a walk in the forest, in the afternoon“ legt die Idiosynkrasie der Modelle offen. „a family at dinner“ überlässt die Menschen dem Modell — Unterbestimmtheit fällt auf demografische Stereotype zurück (Fraser et al. 2023, „A Friendly Face: Do Text-to-Image Systems Rely on Stereotypes when the Input is Under-Specified?“, arXiv:2302.07159; Park 2024, „White Default: Examining Racialized Biases Behind AI-Generated Images“, https://doi.org/10.1080/00043125.2024.2330340). „a street in the evening“ nennt keinen Ort — unterbestimmte Orte bilden überwiegend die Umgebung der USA ab (Basu et al. 2023, „Inspecting the Geographical Representativeness of Images from Text-to-Image Models“, arXiv:2305.11080). „a nurse at work“ neben „a plumber at work“: die Bilder eines Berufs korrelieren mit den US-Erwerbszahlen (Luccioni et al. 2023, „Stable Bias: Evaluating Societal Representations in Diffusion Models“, arXiv:2303.11408), und gewöhnliche Prompts ohne demografische Wörter verstärken Stereotype (Bianchi et al. 2023, „Easily Accessible Text-to-Image Generation Amplifies Demographic Stereotypes at Large Scale“, arXiv:2211.03759). Wer Verstärkung misst, muss Vergleichbares vergleichen: die scheinbare Verstärkung schrumpft, wenn Trainingsbeschriftungen und Prompts dieselbe Verteilung haben (Seshadri et al. 2023, „The Bias Amplification Paradox in Text-to-Image Generation“, arXiv:2308.00755).

goals.competence: Engage 3 — Evaluate whether AI outputs should be accepted, revised or rejected.
goals.expectation: Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations.
goals.classroom: In small groups, learners plan an itinerary for a tourist visiting their hometown. When the teacher provides AI-generated recommendations for local restaurants, learners compare the recommendations using other sources to determine if the information is outdated, inaccurate or a “hallucination.” From there, learners draw from their own knowledge and experience to decide whether the locations would be appealing to a visitor.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme prüft KI-Empfehlungen an anderen Quellen auf Veraltetes, Falsches und Erfundenes. Beim Modell-Vergleich steht unter den erzeugten Spalten die Reihe „Ergebnisse zu diesem Prompt“: ein Sprachmodell kürzt den Prompt auf einen Suchbegriff, der angezeigt wird, und Wikimedia Commons liefert dazu bis zu drei wirkliche Fotografien mit Urheber und Lizenz. Der Gegenstand wechselt von Restaurantempfehlungen zu Bildern eines wirklichen Ortes oder Dings.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe wählt ein Wahrzeichen ihres Ortes als Prompt. Sie vergleicht die erzeugten Bilder mit den Commons-Fotos darunter und notiert je Modell, was stimmt, was veraltet oder falsch ist und was erfunden wurde. Dann entscheidet sie aus eigener Kenntnis des Ortes, welches Bild einem Besucher etwas Richtiges zeigt.

goals.competence: Engage 7 — Analyse how well the use of an AI system aligns with ethical principles and human values.
goals.expectation: Learners identify when AI use may have unintended impacts or implications that are different from a user’s immediate goals.
goals.classroom: Learners analyse a case study where an AI tool uses one’s browsing history to advertise discounts and sales on products they have viewed in the past. With their teacher, learners weigh the opportunities to save money with risks the AI tool poses for personal privacy. They discuss the pros and cons of using the tool in the long- and short-term.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme wägt an einem Fall (Werbung aus dem Browserverlauf) den Vorteil gegen das Risiko für die Privatsphäre ab. Der Fall der Plattform ist der eigene Prompt: beim Modell-Vergleich hält das Set „Aktuelle Modelle“ neben zwei lokalen Modellen eines, das bei Google läuft (Gemini 3 Pro, in der Liste mit „€“ gekennzeichnet; der Kasten unter der Vorbereitungsspalte sagt, dass ein Bild dort auf eine Anfrage an Google Search zurückgreifen kann), das Set „SD-Historie“ drei lokale Modelle. Die DSGVO-Marke in der Kopfzeile nennt die Anbieter-Voreinstellung der Installation.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt denselben Prompt einmal mit „SD-Historie“ und einmal mit „Aktuelle Modelle“ laufen und wägt danach ab: Was hat das Modell bei Google besser gemacht, und was hat der Prompt dafür verlassen? Die DSGVO-Marke sagt, welche Anbieter-Voreinstellung diese Installation hat.

goals.competence: Create 2 — Visualise, prototype and combine ideas using different types of AI systems.
goals.expectation: Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs.
goals.classroom: Learners design a concept to share about a new club at their school. They generate multiple mission statements, activity ideas and visual styles using text and image generators. Then they compare how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.
goals.how_de: Der Modell-Vergleich legt denselben Prompt zwei bis fünf Bildmodellen vor, mit derselben Startzahl über den Spalten („Seed“); was auseinandergeht, liegt an den Modellen. Solange ein Set gewählt ist, steht am Fuß der Vorbereitungsspalte ein Kasten dazu, wofür der Hersteller jedes Modell gebaut hat.
goals.practice_de: Der Club-Prompt läuft über die Modelle eines Sets; die Gruppe beschreibt je Spalte, welche Auslegung das Modell gewählt hat, und liest im Kasten nach, wofür der Hersteller das Modell gebaut hat.

goals.competence: Shape 1 — Investigate how an AI system is intended to work, whom it is designed for and what its limitations are.
goals.expectation: Learners identify what different AI systems are designed to do.
goals.classroom: Learners review model cards that describe how an AI system works, its training data, intended uses and possible limitations. As a class, they discuss appropriate uses of the AI system.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme liest Modellkarten (Arbeitsweise, Trainingsdaten, vorgesehene Nutzung, Grenzen) und bespricht angemessene Nutzung. Der Modell-Vergleich trägt am Fuß der Vorbereitungsspalte, solange ein Set gewählt ist, einen Kasten, der sagt, wofür der Hersteller jedes Modell gebaut hat, in dessen eigenen Worten aus dem Paper oder der Veröffentlichung, mit Quellen darunter. Von den vier Punkten der Modellkarte deckt der Kasten die vorgesehene Nutzung.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe liest den Kasten für die drei Modelle eines Sets und schreibt je Modell einen Satz, wofür es gebaut ist. Dann lässt sie einen Prompt laufen, der genau das verlangt (etwa lesbare Schrift im Bild), und prüft, ob das Modell hält, was der Hersteller sagt.

goals.competence: Shape 2 — Evaluate AI systems using defined criteria, expected outcomes, test cases and user feedback.
goals.expectation: Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task.
goals.classroom: Learners examine an AI system that recommends new music. In small groups, they define criteria for what would make the system successful and compare the system’s recommendations for users with different interests or interaction histories.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme definiert Kriterien, wann ein Musik-Empfehlungssystem seine Aufgabe erfüllt, und vergleicht Empfehlungen für verschiedene Nutzer. Das Empfehlungssystem wird durch ein Bildmodell ersetzt: der Modell-Vergleich hält alles außer dem Modell fest (ein Prompt, eine Startzahl über den Spalten), so dass die Kriterien der Gruppe an mehreren Systemen zugleich geprüft werden.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt vor dem Lauf drei Kriterien auf, woran sie erkennt, dass ein Bild den Prompt erfüllt hat. Dann läuft der Prompt über die Modelle, und die Gruppe bewertet jede Spalte nach ihren Kriterien; die verschiedenen Nutzer der Maßnahme werden durch drei verschiedene Prompts ersetzt.

goals.expectation: Learners understand why AI-generated outputs should be verified and recognise how they can verify the content themselves.
goals.classroom: Learners review an AI-powered tool’s solution to a maths problem and accompanying explanation, then compare the AI-generated content to the process that their teacher has introduced to the class.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme vergleicht die Lösung eines KI-Werkzeugs mit einem Verfahren, das die Klasse kennt, damit klar wird, warum Ausgaben geprüft werden und wie man selbst prüft. Beim Sprachverständnis ist die prüfbare Ausgabe die Übersetzung: über jeder Spalte steht die Übersetzung, die an die Modelle ging, und ihre Rückübersetzung in die eigene Sprache. Das Verfahren, das die Klasse kennt, ist ihre eigene Sprache; die Mathematikaufgabe der Maßnahme wird durch die Übersetzung ersetzt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt eine Bildbeschreibung in ihrer Sprache und lässt sie in drei weiteren laufen. Vor dem Blick auf die Bilder prüft sie die Rückübersetzung: Wo weicht sie ab, und hätte die Gruppe die Abweichung ohne die Rückübersetzung bemerkt? Erst dann schreibt sie Unterschiede zwischen den Bildern den Modellen zu.

goals.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
goals.classroom: Learners explore how and why facial recognition technology performs differently across demographics and discuss possible real-world impacts when it is used for decision making in everyday life.
goals.how_de: Dieselbe Frage an der Sprache: beim Sprachverständnis läuft dieselbe Bildbeschreibung in bis zu vier von zwanzig Sprachen, darunter Obersorbisch, Yorùbá und Runasimi, durch dieselben Bildmodelle, eines je Reihe.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt eine Beschreibung ohne Ortsangabe, lässt sie in ihrer Sprache und in drei weiteren laufen und benennt je Bild, was das Modell aus der Sprache gemacht hat, das in der Beschreibung nie stand.

goals.expectation: Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them.
goals.classroom: When their teacher presents different AI-generated interpretations of a historical event, learners turn to trusted secondary or primary sources to verify the accuracy of the interpretations and argue which one they would include in a final report.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme stellt mehrere KI-Deutungen desselben Ereignisses nebeneinander, prüft sie an Quellen und begründet, welche in einen Bericht kommt. Das Bildverständnis stellt mehrere Lesarten desselben Bildes nebeneinander: mehrere Modelle, eine gewählte Lesart als Anweisung (unter anderem „Kritische Lesart“), das Feld bleibt beschreibbar. Das Ereignis wird durch ein Bild ersetzt, zu dem die Klasse Quellen hat.
goals.practice_de: Die Kursleitung wählt ein Kunstwerk oder ein historisches Foto, zu dem es Quellen gibt, und lässt es von mehreren Modellen unter derselben Lesart lesen. Die Gruppe prüft jede Lesung an den Quellen, streicht Behauptungen, die dort nicht gedeckt sind, und begründet, welche Lesung sie für einen Bericht übernimmt, überarbeitet oder verwirft.

technical.what:
1) eSpeak NG 1.51.1 (1995): the computer voice from before AI. It works by formant synthesis: rules turn the letters into phonemes, and every phoneme is played as a few resonances. Cf. "speak", Jonathan Duddington, 1995.

2) Piper 1.6.0 (2022): parallel (VITS, 2021: the model forms each sentence in one pass and samples pitch and rhythm anew at every run). Every voice is one model file, trained on a recorded dataset, for most of the installed voices by fine-tuning an English base voice. What can be chosen is which voice model speaks, and the speaker heard is the recorded one. (Michael Hansen, Rhasspy project, 2022; the installed 1.6.0 from the Home Assistant authors, 2026) In the German voice "mls", 236 speakers are trained into one model file. Piper speaks with one of them per run. They are volunteers who recorded public-domain books for LibriVox. The research corpus Multilingual LibriSpeech holds their recordings. Under "Speaker", the drop-down names each of them by their number in the corpus, with their index in the file in brackets, and adds gender and the amount recorded as the corpus documents them.

3) Supertonic 3 (2026): 99 million parameters; non-autoregressive (a passage is formed in one pass). A flow-matching decoder over a speech autoencoder. Ten voices are trained as vectors into the model. They can be mixed by simple addition and normalization, e.g. v = (v(F1) + v(F3) + v(M4)) / 3. (Supertone, 2026)

4) VoxCPM2 (2026): 2 billion parameters; diffusion-autoregressive (each piece is denoised into place and conditions how the one after it is read, across sentence boundaries too). No parameters; the whole input is read as language, directions about the voice are embedded in the prompt and are understood. (OpenBMB, 2026)
technical.technical:
eSpeak NG 1.51.1 (from "speak", Jonathan Duddington, 1995) - the computer voice from before AI. Formant synthesis: rules turn the letters into phonemes, and every phoneme is played as a few resonances. No recording of anybody is in it, which is why it fits into a few megabytes and speaks over a hundred languages.

Piper 1.6.0 (Michael Hansen, Rhasspy project, 2022; the installed 1.6.0 is from the Home Assistant authors, 2026), VITS (Kim et al., 2021), non-autoregressive (each sentence is formed in one pass, no piece waiting on the one before; longer input is cut at sentence boundaries and each sentence is spoken on its own): every voice is one model file, trained on a recorded dataset, for most of the installed voices by fine-tuning an English base voice (each voice’s MODEL_CARD says which). What can be chosen is which voice model speaks. The speaker heard is the recorded one; pitch and rhythm are sampled anew at every run, which VITS was built for: "a text input can be spoken in multiple ways with different pitches and rhythms" (Kim et al., 2021, abstract).

Supertonic 3 (Supertone, 2026), about 99M parameters, non-autoregressive (a passage is formed in one pass, no piece waiting on the one before; longer input is cut at sentence boundaries into passages of at most 300 characters and each is spoken on its own): a flow-matching decoder over a speech autoencoder. Ten voices are trained as vectors into the model. They can be mixed by simple addition and normalization, e.g. v = (v(F1) + v(F3) + v(M4)) / 3.

VoxCPM2 (OpenBMB, 2026), 2B parameters, tokenizer-free and diffusion-autoregressive (each piece is denoised into place, and what stands there conditions the next): the prompt is read as language rather than as settings. The expression is described in words within the prompt (there are no technical parameters to manipulate emotional expression in this model).
technical.brief: Four text-to-speech systems asked the same sentence side by side - eSpeak NG (1995), Piper (2022), Supertonic 3 (2026), VoxCPM2 (2026) - with an eye to how they stage emotion and gender. What each can be asked for is a different kind of thing: a setting of the formant rules, a choice of voice file trained on a recording, a mixture of ten voice vectors, or a description written into the sentence itself. Every recording stays in the column of the machine that made it.

goals.competence: Engage 2 — Describe how AI systems perform tasks using language that addresses and clarifies common misconceptions.
goals.expectation: Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding.
goals.classroom: Learners review different types of AI tools and compare design choices that make the systems appear human-like, friendly or intelligent. In small groups, learners practise explaining how the tools produce outputs, focussing on programmed processes rather than human qualities. As a class, they share and refine their explanations and reflect on how different design features affect understanding and trust in AI systems.
goals.how_de: Beim Stimmen-Vergleich ist die Menschenähnlichkeit selbst der Entwurf: eine Regelmaschinerie von 1995 (eSpeak NG) mit zwölf Einstellungen, in der keine Aufnahme steckt, neben drei trainierten Systemen (Supertonic 3, VoxCPM2, Piper). Bei Supertonic stehen die Stimmen unter F1 bis F5 und M1 bis M5 mit einer Beschreibung und der gemessenen Tonhöhe in Hz; bei VoxCPM2 wird die sprechende Person in drei Auswahlfeldern (Geschlecht, Alter, Ausdruck) beschrieben.
goals.practice_de: Dieselbe Zeile in allen Spalten; die Gruppe ordnet die Stimmen nach „klingt wie ein Mensch“ und erklärt danach je Spalte, wie der Klang zustande kommt (Regeln; zehn als Vektoren ins Modell trainierte Stimmen; eine Beschreibung aus drei Auswahlfeldern; Aufnahmen), ohne den Systemen Absicht oder Gefühl zuzuschreiben.

goals.competence: Manage 2 — Choose an appropriate AI approach for a task by comparing how different AI systems operate and what they are best suited to do.
goals.expectation: Learners recognise that some types of AI systems can be programmed with specific rules to accomplish tasks, while others can learn patterns from data.
goals.classroom: Learners compare different approaches to building AI systems by completing a trash-sorting task. First, they consider why random outputs would be unlikely to reliably sort items. Next, they direct a classmate role-playing as a robot to sort images of trash based on specific criteria. They observe how the “robot” responds to new images that do not match the criteria. Finally, they explore how a system could use patterns from collected data, such as a class survey, to improve sorting decisions and determine which approach is most appropriate for different tasks.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme vergleicht Ansätze für eine Sortieraufgabe: Zufall, feste Regeln (ein Mitschüler als Roboter) und Muster aus Daten. Das Rollenspiel ist analog; für den letzten Schritt, wie ein System mit Mustern aus Daten arbeitet und welcher Ansatz zu welcher Aufgabe passt, stellt der Stimmen-Vergleich die Systeme nebeneinander: eine Regelmaschinerie von 1995 (eSpeak NG) mit zwölf Einstellungen, in der keine Aufnahme steckt, und drei trainierte Systeme, die dieselbe Zeile sprechen. Die Sortieraufgabe wird durch das Sprechen einer Zeile ersetzt.
goals.practice_de: Nach dem Rollenspiel schreibt die Gruppe eine Zeile mit einem schwierigen Wort (einem Namen, einem Fremdwort) und hört sie in allen Spalten. Sie beschreibt, was die Regelmaschine daraus macht und was die trainierten Stimmen, und ordnet dann Aufgaben zu: Wo reichen Regeln, wo braucht es Muster aus Daten?

goals.competence: Manage 2 — Choose an appropriate AI approach for a task by comparing how different AI systems operate and what they are best suited to do.
goals.expectation: Learners identify the benefits and drawbacks of using a rules-based approach and a machine learning approach to solve a problem.
goals.classroom: Learners compare technology that follows set rules to execute a task (e.g. calculators, traffic lights, thermostats) with technologies that have been trained on examples from data (e.g., image recognition, translation). With a teacher, they consider why each approach suits the specific task.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme vergleicht Technik mit festen Regeln (Taschenrechner, Ampel) mit trainierter Technik (Bilderkennung, Übersetzung) und fragt, warum jeder Ansatz zu seiner Aufgabe passt. Der Stimmen-Vergleich hat beides an derselben Aufgabe: die Regelmaschinerie von 1995 (eSpeak NG) und drei trainierte Systeme (Supertonic 3 mit zehn Stimmen unter F1 bis M5; VoxCPM2, dem die sprechende Person in drei Auswahlfeldern beschrieben wird; Piper mit aufgenommenen Stimmen nach Sprache, und wo eine Datei mehrere Sprecher trägt, mit der Wahl des Sprechers). Jede Spalte trägt Name und Jahr ihres Systems und seine Auswahlfelder.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe sammelt die Beispiele der Kursleitung an der Tafel, hört dann dieselbe Zeile in allen Spalten und trägt den Stimmen-Vergleich als weiteres Beispielpaar ein: Was kann die Regelmaschine, was die trainierten nicht können, und umgekehrt?

goals.competence: Shape 1 — Investigate how an AI system is intended to work, whom it is designed for and what its limitations are.
goals.expectation: Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool.
goals.classroom: Learners examine several examples of AI tools (e.g. a chatbot, recommendation system or route-planning app). For each, learners identify its primary task and explain in simple terms what input it uses and how the outputs execute the task.
goals.how_de: Beim Stimmen-Vergleich trägt jede Spalte Name und Jahr ihres Systems und seine Auswahlfelder; die vier Systeme haben dieselbe Aufgabe und verschiedene Eingaben (zwölf Einstellungen; zehn Stimmen mit Tonhöhe in Hz; drei Auswahlfelder zur sprechenden Person; Sprache und Stimme aus Aufnahmen, bei einer Datei mit mehreren Sprechern auch der Sprecher).
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt je Spalte auf, was hineingeht und was herauskommt, und erklärt in einfachen Worten, wie die Ausgabe die Aufgabe erledigt.

technical.brief: A written prompt, put to the chosen image models in one run: as it stands, and again with a culture or a country named in it. Every run includes the prompt without any such addition, and nothing rewrites it on the way to the model.
technical.what: Several image models receive the base prompt once on its own and beside it with a culture or a country named in it — "Yoruba", "Sámi", "Franconian". The rows hold the models, the columns the variations, and a model computes in its row with the same seed and with exactly this wording.
technical.how: The first column shows what a model brings out while the prompt says nothing about origin: which place, which people, which clothing count to it as the obvious ones. The further columns show what a named culture changes: whether the model shows the practice meant, or only swaps the surroundings and delivers the cliché. If you choose only 1 model, 5 different variations (seeds) are used, so that you can compare a range of results.

goals.competence: Engage 6 — Explain how AI could be used to amplify societal biases.
goals.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
goals.classroom: Learners explore how and why facial recognition technology performs differently across demographics and discuss possible real-world impacts when it is used for decision making in everyday life.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme untersucht, warum eine Technik über Bevölkerungsgruppen hinweg verschieden gut arbeitet, am Beispiel Gesichtserkennung. Bei der Stereotypen-Analyse ist die Technik ein Bildmodell und die Gruppe eine Kultur: ein Basis-Prompt mit einem Platzhalter „*“, in den je Spalte ein Wort eingesetzt wird („Yoruba“, „Sámi“, „Franconian“), die erste Spalte ohne Einsetzung, jede Zeile ein Modell, alle Bilder einer Zeile mit derselben Startzahl. Die Folgen für Entscheidungen im Alltag bespricht die Kursleitung.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe wählt eine Alltagsszene (ein Frühstück, eine Hochzeit) als Basis-Prompt und liest das Raster: Wer ist in der ersten Spalte selbstverständlich? Welche Kultur trifft das Modell, welche wird zur Kulisse? Sie hält je Zelle fest, was zutrifft und was Klischee ist.

goals.competence: Engage 6 — Explain how AI could be used to amplify societal biases.
goals.expectation: Learners analyse how individuals, companies or institutions may build and deploy AI systems to serve particular interests and how these systems might shape opportunities, representations or public perceptions.
goals.classroom: With a teacher, learners evaluate real-world examples of AI being used to influence an event (e.g. misinformation and disinformation on social media). Then they explore how an institution’s choices regarding AI use might benefit certain groups while having a negative effect on others.
goals.how_de: Wie ein Modell Repräsentationen prägt, ist der Gegenstand des Rasters der Stereotypen-Analyse (siehe Mittelstufe): welcher Ort, welche Menschen, welche Kleidung ihm als das Selbstverständliche gelten, solange im Satz von Herkunft nichts steht.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe wählt einen Beruf oder ein Fest als Basis-Prompt, liest die erste Spalte des Rasters für die Modelle und bespricht, wer dort als Regel erscheint und welche Gruppen nur mit ausdrücklicher Nennung vorkommen.

goals.competence: Shape 2 — Evaluate AI systems using defined criteria, expected outcomes, test cases and user feedback.
goals.expectation: Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task.
goals.classroom: Learners examine an AI system that recommends new music. In small groups, they define criteria for what would make the system successful and compare the system’s recommendations for users with different interests or interaction histories.
goals.how_de: Das Raster der Stereotypen-Analyse vergleicht je Zeile ein Modell und je Spalte ein eingesetztes Wort, jedes Bild einer Zeile mit derselben Startzahl; die verschiedenen Nutzer werden durch die Kulturen in den Spalten ersetzt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe legt vorher fest, woran sie erkennt, dass ein Modell die gemeinte Praxis trifft, und prüft das Raster Zelle für Zelle daran.

technical.what: Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same prompt, once per writing model. Write the prompt, choose the perspective it is to be written through, and tick the models that are to write; one image model puts a picture beside each text. The top row holds the prompt as it was written, and what the image model makes of it with that step left out.
technical.how: This instrument compares texts; the picture beside a text is what one image model made of it. Between two rows the writing model is the only difference: the prompt, the perspective, the adaption each image model carries and the seed are the same for every row.
technical.brief: The same line, written by one model after another

Die Werkzeuge der Maßnahme werden durch die Sprachmodelle ersetzt, die unter einer Perspektive schreiben.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt den Club-Prompt unter einer Perspektive über die Sprachmodelle laufen, liest je Zeile den Text und vergleicht, wie jedes Modell die Idee ausgelegt hat, mit dem Bild als Lesehilfe.

technical.what: Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same template, once per perspective, and one image model shows what each of them wrote. Write the template — or drag a picture onto the field, and its description then stands there as the template, where it can be worked on further. Choose the perspectives. Where the template was written, the first picture holds it with that step left out; where it was read from a picture, that picture stands first as the reference and the picture beside it is the first step, with no perspective on it; resting on a perspective — holding it, on a touch screen — shows the text that perspective wrote.
technical.how: Every picture carries the same template, and between two of them the perspective is the only difference, so a picture can be read for what that one perspective does to the template. The writing model is the one this platform is set to intercept with, and this surface makes no choice about it. One image model runs, because what is compared here is perspectives — the comparison of image models is its own instrument.
technical.brief: The same template, written through one perspective after another
technical.reading: Die Vorlage ist das WAS, die gewählte Perspektive das WIE. Dieselbe Idee, durch verschiedene Regeln beschrieben, ergibt verschiedene Bilder — die Trennung macht die Regel als Gestaltungsentscheidung sichtbar, die in einem gemischten Prompt unsichtbar bliebe (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md, Abschnitt 1). Der Eintrag „forest“ der zentralen Preset-Liste („a walk in the forest, seen through the eyes of a child“, Eigenschaften-Katalog Nr. 4, UCD-118 Plan Rev. 3) lässt sich hier auswerten — in das freie Feld geschrieben; die Auswahl daneben trägt bewusst nur „house“: der Satz benennt sein WAS und darin eine Rolle, die sagt, wer sieht; die Perspektivenliste liefert das WIE.

technical.what: One aesthetic checklist, set property by property, and what a model writes from it and the template. Write the template — or drag a picture onto the field, and its description then stands there as the template. Every property that can carry a handle is a scale of words with one handle on it; a property left at its neutral word stays out of the prompt. Five chips over the bars set the whole checklist at once, and from there each property is moved on its own. One setting is one prompt. Every run adds a row, and the first row stays: the checklist at its neutral word throughout, which every picture beside it is read against. Where the template was read from a picture, that picture stands first as the reference, and the picture beside it is the first step, with no setting on it. One image model runs, so what parts two pictures is the setting. Resting on a picture's name — holding it — shows what was set and what the model wrote from it.
technical.how: The properties come from the human labelling guidelines of VisionReward, where each of them carries one ordered list of words with one of those words marked as the neutral one. Those guidelines give one position on such a list, which is why there is one handle here. The lists are of different lengths and reach different distances to either side, so each property is set on its own rather than by one axis over all of them, and a setting is free to stand at the good end of one property and at the bad end of the next. Every row is written by the same model from the same template, so what stands between two rows is the setting, and the pictures show what the checklist does to a template.
technical.brief: One template, an aesthetic checklist set property by property, and a row for every setting

goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt ihre Vorlage zum Thema, verstellt eine Eigenschaft und lässt laufen, dann eine zweite; sie liest je Zeile den umgeschriebenen Prompt und das Bild und vergleicht die Zeilen miteinander.

goals.classroom: Learners design a concept to share about a new club at their school. They generate multiple mission statements, activity ideas and visual styles using text and image generators. Then they compare how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.

goals.expectation: Learners know how to prompt AI systems to generate accurate feedback and helpful responses to an idea.
goals.classroom: Learners are shown two different versions of a prompt designed to get feedback on the same idea. They compare AI-generated responses to the two prompts and analyse which prompt led to an output with more accurate or useful feedback. Then they explain what features (e.g. context, specificity, constraints) made it more effective.
goals.how_de: Bei den Ästhetischen Polen sind die zwei Fassungen zwei Einstellungen der Eigenschaftsliste, aus denen ein Sprachmodell je einen Prompt schreibt; die Rückmeldung der Maßnahme wird durch das Bild ersetzt, das jede Zeile zu ihrem Prompt zeigt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt zwei Einstellungen laufen, liest die beiden umgeschriebenen Prompts untereinander und vergleicht, was sich im Prompt und was sich im Bild geändert hat.

technical.brief: Eight tools for investigating how diffusion models generate images from text. They sort by where they intervene.
technical.hints: Eight tools for investigating how diffusion models generate images from text. They sort by where they intervene. The text encoders turn your prompt into one fixed embedding, and that same embedding then guides all 25 denoising steps. Dimension Explorer, Concept Algebra and Encoder Fusion change the embedding once, before the loop starts, and the Encoder Fusion Workbench sweeps the fusion parameters across three axes. Composable Diffusion stands in both places: it combines what the model returns at each single step, or interpolates between the concepts’ embeddings before the loop starts. Denoising Archaeology and Attention Cartography change nothing and only look. Mean Images leaves the model alone as well and averages many pictures into one. For the two SD 3.5 models it averages the latents of those pictures, before the decoder.

technical.brief: Observe every single denoising step.
technical.what: A diffusion model creates an image by progressively removing noise. Unlike drawing from left to right, the model works on ALL image regions simultaneously. In the first steps, rough structures emerge: Where is up, where is down? Where is the horizon? In the middle steps, semantic content appears: objects, shapes, colors. The final steps refine textures and details. This tool makes every single step visible.
technical.how: Enter a prompt and start the run with the triangle in the bar above the surface. The model produces one intermediate image per denoising step. One of them fills the view at a time; the slider in the left column names the sections of the run, and moving along it steps from one image to the next. Compare early and late steps: at which step does the picture turn from noise into a scene?
technical.reading: Early steps: Global composition — basic structure, color distribution, layout planning. Middle steps: Semantic emergence — objects become recognizable, shapes crystallize. Late steps: Detail refinement — textures, edges, fine patterns. The transitions are gradual, and the three zones are working coordinates, not verified boundaries: Choi et al. (2022) hypothesise a coarse / content / clean-up division, but they locate it by noise level, not by step number, and they measure it during training, not in a generation run. Particularly revealing: The very first step does not show fine-grained pixels, but colorful patches. This is because the noise is generated in latent space (128×128 at 16 channels), not in pixel space. The VAE translates each latent pixel into an ~8×8 pixel patch — even pure Gaussian noise becomes coherent color clusters. The computation runs in this compressed space throughout, rather than on individual pixels.
technical.technical: Two backbones run here: SD 3.5 Large, a rectified-flow transformer whose one scheduler is FlowMatchEuler, and SDXL, a U-Net whose scheduler is picked from a list. SD 3.5 additionally carries a shift, which spreads the steps over the noise scale; its own scheduler config sets that to 3.0. 25 steps are preset. At each step the current latent vectors are decoded through the VAE (Variational Autoencoder), which translates the mathematical latent space into pixels. The latent representation is 128×128 across 16 channels — each latent point corresponds to a patch of about 8×8 pixels in the image. This is why even the first step shows colour clusters instead of fine pixel noise: the VAE translates random 16-dimensional vectors into coherent colour fields. The view shows the noisy intermediate state decoded through the VAE, rather than the model's prediction of the finished image — Ho et al. (2020) show that prediction in their own figures.
technical.hints: Observe every single denoising step. Diffusion models don't draw left-to-right — they work everywhere simultaneously, from rough shapes to fine detail.

goals.competence: Engage 2 — Describe how AI systems perform tasks using language that addresses and clarifies common misconceptions.
goals.expectation: Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding.
goals.classroom: As their teacher introduces common phrases used to describe AI use (e.g. “AI thinks,” “AI understands,”), learners identify which ones are misleading and why. Learners develop better descriptions using technically accurate and age-appropriate language, then reflect on how language shapes their understanding of what AI can or cannot do.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme prüft Redeweisen wie „die KI denkt“ oder „die KI versteht“ darauf, welche irreführend sind, und ersetzt sie durch technisch zutreffende Beschreibungen. Denoising Archaeology liefert den Gegenstand für die Beschreibung: jeden Entrauschungsschritt eines Laufs als eigenes Bild (voreingestellt 25 Schritte). Die Redeweisen bringt die Kursleitung mit; die Beschreibungen schreiben die Lernenden.
goals.practice_de: Die Kursleitung sammelt an der Tafel, wie die Gruppe über Bild-KI spricht („sie malt“, „sie weiß, wie ein Haus aussieht“). Die Gruppe lässt einen eigenen Prompt durch Denoising Archaeology laufen, geht die Schritte durch und schreibt zu jeder Redeweise, was an den Schritten zu sehen ist und was der Satz behauptet. Dann formuliert sie den Satz neu, ohne Malen, Wissen und Wollen.

goals.competence: Engage 2 — Describe how AI systems perform tasks using language that addresses and clarifies common misconceptions.
goals.expectation: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
goals.classroom: Learners identify a common AI myth among peers (e.g. “AI understands like humans” or “AI is always correct”). They create an artefact, such as a poster, short video or podcast to address the misconception by explaining how AI works.
goals.how_de: Für den Mythos „die KI malt Strich für Strich“ liefert Denoising Archaeology die Einzelschritte eines Laufs als Bildreihe für das Artefakt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe wählt fünf Schritte aus, setzt sie in der Reihenfolge auf das Plakat und schreibt zu jedem, was darin schon zu sehen ist und was noch fehlt.

technical.brief: Many generated images, from rewordings of one prompt or from one prompt on different seeds, averaged into one picture. For the two SD 3.5 models the mean is taken before the decoder, and each row says which mean it shows.
technical.what: The instrument generates many images from one prompt and averages them into one mean image, per AI model. Two means are computed per model. The first is the mean of the images generated from English variants of the prompt, which a language model writes with the same content in other words, as many as the setting ‘Images per cell’ says. The second is the mean of the images generated from the prompt as entered on randomly varied starting seeds. The models are selectable, one row each; both columns always stand. A switch in the left column shows the single images as a contact sheet, or a relief of the mean, instead. For the two SD 3.5 models the mean is taken before the decoder: the latents of the pictures are averaged and decoded once. The other models are averaged pixel by pixel, and each row says which.
technical.how: This page applies the artist Hito Steyerl’s ‘mean images’ as a method against generative AI models. The mean of many images, generated from rewordings of one prompt or from one prompt on different seeds, can be compared across AI models. The comparison serves the exploration of visual clichés, prejudices and other forms of the statistical production of ‘normality’.
technical.reading: Die promptFixed-Achse hält den Satz fest und wandert mit den Startzahlen: was im Mittelbild stehen bleibt, ist der Effekt des Prompts, nicht der einer einzelnen Startzahl. Für die Sätze der zentralen Liste (Eigenschaften-Katalog, UCD-118 Plan Rev. 3) heißt das — das Feld nimmt jeden Satz an, die Auswahl daneben trägt nur „house“ und „street“: „friendship“ und „loneliness“ sind abstrakte Begriffe ohne jede weitere Angabe — das Mittel vieler Bilder zeigt das eine Klischee, in das das Modell den Begriff übersetzt (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md: „Abstrakte Konzepte werden oft in Klischees übersetzt“; die DIM-Metrik des DIMCIM-Rahmens beziffert, wie wenig die Erzeugung ohne ausdrückliche Angabe variiert: Teotia et al. 2025, „DIMCIM: A Quantitative Evaluation Framework for Default-mode Diversity and Generalization in Text-to-Image Generative Models“, arXiv:2506.05108). „a family at dinner“ überlässt die Menschen dem Modell, „a street in the evening“ den Ort — Unterbestimmtheit fällt auf Defaults: demografische Stereotype bei Trait-Wörtern ohne demografische Angabe (Fraser et al. 2023, arXiv:2302.07159; Park 2024, https://doi.org/10.1080/00043125.2024.2330340), die Umgebung der USA bei Orten ohne Ortsangabe (Basu et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.11080). „a nurse at work“ und „a plumber at work“ zeigen im Mittel die Lesart, in die das Modell für einen Beruf fällt (Luccioni et al. 2023, arXiv:2303.11408; Bianchi et al. 2023, arXiv:2211.03759).

goals.how_de: Für den Mythos „jedes KI-Bild ist einzigartig“ liefert Mean Images je Modell den Mittelwert vieler Bilder zu einem Prompt: einmal aus Umformulierungen des Prompts, die ein Sprachmodell inhaltsgleich schreibt, einmal aus demselben Prompt auf verschiedenen Startzahlen; bei den beiden SD 3.5-Modellen wird der Mittelwert vor dem Decoder gebildet.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt ihren Prompt als Serie laufen, setzt das mean image neben drei der Einzelbilder auf das Plakat und erklärt, was ein Mittelwert aus Bildern ist und was in ihm übrig bleibt.

goals.competence: Engage 6 — Explain how AI could be used to amplify societal biases.
goals.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
goals.classroom: Learners explore how and why facial recognition technology performs differently across demographics and discuss possible real-world impacts when it is used for decision making in everyday life.
goals.how_de: Mean Images mittelt viele Bilder je Modell zu einem Bild: aus Umformulierungen eines Prompts oder aus einem Prompt auf verschiedenen Startzahlen; die Seite nennt als Zweck die Erkundung visueller Klischees, Vorurteile und anderer Formen der statistischen Produktion von ‚Normalität‘. Die Bevölkerungsgruppe der Maßnahme wird durch das Motiv des Prompts ersetzt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe schreibt einen Prompt zu einer Rolle oder einem Beruf, lässt die Serie über zwei Modelle laufen und vergleicht je Modell das mean image mit den Einzelbildern.

technical.brief: For each word in the prompt, a heatmap overlay on the generated image shows WHERE in the image that word had the most influence.
technical.what: When a diffusion model generates an image, it does not read the prompt word by word. Instead, a mechanism called "attention" distributes the influence of each word across different image regions. The word "house" mainly influences the region where the house appears — but also neighboring areas, because the model understands the context of the entire scene. This tool makes that distribution visible: a clicked word shows the image regions it influences most.
technical.how: Bright, intense color = strong influence of the word on that region. Dark or absent color = little influence. If you select multiple words, they appear in different colors. Note: the maps are NOT perfectly sharp-edged — this is not a bug, but shows that the model processes concepts contextually, not in isolation. A "house" in a farm scene also has some influence on animals and fields, because the model understands the scene as a whole.
technical.reading: The denoising step slider shows WHEN in the 25-step generation process you are viewing attention. Early steps show rough layout planning, late steps show detail assignment. The network depth selector shows WHERE in the transformer attention is measured: shallow layers (near input) show global composition planning, middle layers semantic assignment, deep layers fine-tuning. Both axes are independent — it is worth systematically exploring different combinations.
technical.technical: SD3.5 uses an MMDiT (Multimodal Diffusion Transformer) with joint attention: image and text tokens attend to each other across 24 transformer blocks. We replace the default SDPA processor with a manual softmax(QK^T/√d) processor at 3 selected blocks to extract the text→image attention submatrix. Maps are 64x64 resolution (patch grid), upscaled to image resolution via bilinear interpolation. SD3.5 has three text encoders — CLIP-L (BPE, 77 tokens), CLIP-G (BPE, 77 tokens) and T5-XXL (SentencePiece, 512 tokens); two of them can be toggled here to see how different tokenization strategies affect attention.
technical.hints:
For each word in the prompt, a heatmap overlay on the generated image shows WHERE in the image that word had the most influence. This reveals how the model spatially distributes semantic concepts.

e.g. A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen.

Click one or more words. Subword tokens (e.g. "Ku"+"gel") are automatically combined. Multiple words appear in different colors.

Diffusion models generate images in 25 steps from noise to image. Early steps establish rough structure, late steps refine details. This slider shows what the model attends to at each step.

At every denoising step, the signal passes through all 24 transformer layers. Shallow layers (near input) capture global composition, middle layers semantic assignment, deep layers (near output) fine details. Both controls are independent: step = when in the process, depth = where in the network.

SD3.5 uses two text encoders with different tokenization. CLIP-L uses BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding), T5-XXL uses SentencePiece. Compare how both encoders process the same prompt and which image regions each one steers.

technical.technical: The arithmetic runs in ComfyUI in the node AI4ArtsEdSD3ThreeFactors (comfyui_nodes/ai4artsed_sd3_conditioning.py), on the parts the encode node of the same family delivers for the prompt: rows 0–76 receive a · CLIP + b · T5[0..76], the rows from 77 on receive c · T5, in float32, nothing clamped. T5 runs at 512 rows (T5TokenizerOptions, min_length 512, devserver/schemas/engine/comfyui_chunk_support.py) or at the prompt’s own length past that. The layout of the block is the fourth parameter, t5_rows: full, rows 0–511 under the CLIP block, a table of 589 rows, or tail, rows 77–511 alone, a table of 512 rows, the layout of the earlier Surrealizer, in which T5’s rows 0–76 reach the model only as the b-fold addend inside the CLIP block. The pooled vector, CLIP-L’s 768 and CLIP-G’s 1280 numbers joined, is the fifth parameter, pooled. Under clip the node hands it on as the two encoders compute it; under zero it hands on zeros of the same shape, which is what ComfyUI itself assembles for the vector when it runs without a CLIP encoder (comfy/text_encoders/sd3_clip.py). The three factors act on the table; the vector passes whole. The negative prompt passes through a second node of the same kind under the same five parameters; an empty negative is the encoding of the empty string. (1, 0, 1, full, clip) is the sequence and the vector as ComfyUI assembles them on its own; (1 − α, α, 1, tail, clip) is the earlier node AI4ArtsEdSD3Fusion under legacy at α, bit for bit, which is what the three Surrealization fields send. Inside the model the whole table passes through one linear layer to the transformer’s width, the same weights for every row, and position encodings are added to the image patches only (Esser et al. 2024, section 4, Figure 2), so a text row’s place in the table plays no part in the computation; a T5 row added into a CLIP row is a sum at that layer’s input. The model reads the pooled vector apart from the table: embeddings of the timestep, the step of the run the model is at, and of this vector are the inputs to the modulation mechanism (Esser et al. 2024, section 4), which every transformer block of the model carries (comfy/ldm/modules/diffusionmodules/mmdit.py), so that zeros in its place change that modulation in every transformer block and leave the table as it is. Esser et al. (2024, “Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis”, ICML 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.03206) describe the assembly in appendix B.2, the CLIP rows zero-padded along the channel axis to 4096 and concatenated along the sequence axis with the T5 rows; the training with each encoder set to zero independently at 46.4 % (B.3); and the ablation without T5 in section 5.3.3, with win rates against the full model of 50 % for aesthetics, 46 % for prompt adherence and 38 % for written text. In the paper the T5 context has 77 rows; ComfyUI runs T5 at 512 rows here. CLIP-L is the text encoder of Radford et al. (2021, “Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision”, ICML 2021, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2103.00020), CLIP-G that of the OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 of Cherti et al. (2023, “Reproducible Scaling Laws for Contrastive Language-Image Learning”, CVPR 2023, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2212.07143), both trained on image–caption pairs; T5-XXL is the encoder of Raffel et al. (2020, “Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer”, JMLR 21, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1910.10683), trained on text alone.
technical.brief: Three factors on the conditioning table of Stable Diffusion 3.5: a on the CLIP block, b for T5’s rows 0–76 added into it, c on the T5 block.
technical.what: Encoder Fusion is an instrument of the Latent Lab that changes the conditioning of the image model Stable Diffusion 3.5 before the model runs: the table of numbers that three text encoders compute from the prompt and that the model computes the picture from. The table has 4096 columns. The two CLIP encoders, CLIP-L and CLIP-G, fill rows 0–76 up to column 2047, and columns 2048–4095 of those rows are zero; the encoder T5-XXL fills 512 rows below across every column, more when the prompt has more T5 pieces, 589 rows in all for a prompt up to that length. A row holds one piece of the prompt, a start or end mark, or padding past the text’s end. CLIP-L and CLIP-G were trained on pairs of images and captions and T5-XXL on text alone, so the two blocks hold two different encodings of the same prompt. Three factors act on the table: a multiplies the CLIP block, c multiplies the T5 block, and b adds T5’s rows 0–76 into the CLIP block cell by cell, each T5 row onto the CLIP row of the same number, whatever piece of the prompt either row holds. The T5 block holds all of those rows or, in the layout of the earlier Surrealizer, rows 77–511 alone, so that T5’s rows 0–76 reach the model only as the b-fold addend inside the CLIP block; the two fields in the line of c set which. Beside the table the model reads the pooled vector, pool in the drawing, CLIP-L’s 768 and CLIP-G’s 1280 numbers joined, as an input of the modulation, the numbers by which each layer of the model scales and shifts what passes through it; the two fields in the line of a set whether the model receives that vector or zeros in its place. Standard, a 1, b 0, c 1, pool CLIP, is the table and the vector as they stand without this instrument. What the instrument is for is the tables beyond that one. With the T5 block zeroed, or with the CLIP block and the pooled vector zeroed, on rows 0–511, the model runs in a state its training contained; a row holding both encodings, which b above 0 produces, or a block with its sign turned, which a below 0 produces, is a conditioning beyond what any prompt produces, and a run shows what the model computes from it. Every run keeps a card under Runs, the strip under the surface, labelled with its three factors, on rows 77–511 with that layout and under zeros in the pooled vector’s place with pool 0, so that runs with different settings stand side by side.
technical.how: Enter a prompt in the field; it goes to CLIP-L, CLIP-G and T5 alike. The six fields over the drawing set all three factors, the layout of the T5 block and the pooled vector, pool in the drawing, at once. CLIP only (a 1, b 0, c 0, pool CLIP) zeroes the T5 block, the setting without T5 that Esser et al. (2024) measured. T5 only (a 0, b 0, c 1, pool 0) zeroes the CLIP block and puts zeros in the pooled vector’s place: the model then runs on T5’s numbers alone. Surrealization 5, 15 and 35 (a 1 − n, b n, c 1, T5 block rows 77–511, pool CLIP) carry the arithmetic of the earlier Surrealizer at its strengths 5, 15 and 35: the CLIP block with its sign turned and stretched, T5’s rows 0–76 added n-fold, and under the CLIP block T5’s rows 77–511 alone. technical.brief: Compare two prompts and discover which embedding dimensions encode the semantic difference.
technical.what: Every word is converted by the text encoder into a high-dimensional vector (e.g. 4096 dimensions for T5). When you change a word in the prompt — e.g. "red" to "blue" — certain dimensions change more than others. This tool shows you WHICH dimensions change most and lets you selectively transfer individual dimensions from prompt B into prompt A.
technical.how: The bar chart shows all dimensions sorted by difference magnitude. Use the rank range controls (From/To) to select a window — e.g. just the top 100 or specifically ranks 880–920. technical.reading: Each bar represents one embedding dimension. The length shows how much that dimension differs between prompt A and B. Dimensions with large differences are the most likely carriers of the semantic change. But note: embeddings are distributed — often multiple dimensions together are needed to produce a visible change.
technical.technical: SD3.5 uses three text encoders: CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d) and T5-XXL (4096d). You can probe each individually. The difference is computed as mean absolute deviation across all token positions: mean(abs(B-A), dim=tokens). The transfer replaces selected dimensions across all token positions simultaneously.

technical.brief: Apply the famous word2vec analogy to image generation: King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.
technical.what: In 2013, Mikolov showed that word embeddings encode semantic relationships as linear directions: the vector for "King" minus "Man" plus "Woman" yields a vector close to "Queen". This tool applies that idea to SD3.5’s text encoders: instead of single words, you manipulate entire prompt embeddings. The result is an image that has moved away from A along the direction B→C. How far it moves, and in what respect, is what the tool lets you look at.
technical.how: You enter three prompts: A (base), B (subtract), and C (add). The formula is: Result = A − Scale₁×B + Scale₂×C. The scale sliders control intensity: at 1.0, B is fully subtracted and C fully added. At 0.5, only half. Values above 1.0 amplify the effect. — Why not just use "A + C" as the prompt and "B" as the negative prompt? Because the two happen in different places. A negative prompt is the baseline that guidance is measured from, so it acts inside the denoising loop, at every one of the 25 steps, against the image as it currently stands. Concept Algebra computes a new vector BEFORE generation: the arithmetic happens in embedding space, once, and the loop never learns that anything was subtracted. — What the subtraction does not do is delete a named object. Our own measurement series on this platform found that subtracting one prompt vector from another shifts tone, framing and register, but leaves the named thing in the picture. Read the result as a displacement in meaning-space, not as a removal.
technical.reading: On the left you see the reference image (prompt A only, same seed). On the right, the algebra result. If the analogy works, the right image should show concept A but with the semantic change B→C. Example: "Sunset at the beach" − "Beach" + "Mountains" ≈ "Sunset over mountains". The L2 distance shows how far the result has moved from the original. — Is the operation commutative? No. Subtraction of B and addition of C happen relative to vector A. The direction B→C only makes sense in the context of A: "King − Man" removes the "male" directions from the King vector, "+ Woman" adds the "female" directions — the result lands near "Queen". C is not surgically placed where B was removed; it is simply added. That this still works shows that semantic relationships are encoded as consistent linear directions in the vector space.
technical.technical: The algebra is performed on the selected encoder embeddings: CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d), T5-XXL (4096d), or all combined (589 tokens × 4096d). The same operation is also applied to pooled embeddings (2048d). Both images use the same seed for fair comparison.

technical.brief: Instead of encoding your entire prompt as one monolithic vector, each concept gets its own transformer pass during denoising.
technical.what: Standard image generation compresses your entire prompt into a single representation. The model sees "a red house by a lake" as one fused concept. Composable Diffusion breaks this apart: "red house" and "lake" each get their own complete processing pass through the neural network at every denoising step. Their predictions are then combined with adjustable weights. This gives each concept its own "energy function" — its own vote on what the image should look like. A concept can also be given a negative weight. Then it is not blended in but subtracted at every step, as its own opposing direction alongside the positive ones. What that achieves depends on what is negated: a thing that appears in the picture as a thing can be pushed out, while a property bound to an object in the positive prompt, or a whole style register, is not removed — the image only recedes, and at high negative weights it loses content and finally over-drives. That is also a different operation from a negative prompt, which replaces the baseline the image is measured against.
technical.how: At each of the 25 denoising steps, the model runs N+1 transformer passes: one for the negative prompt (unconditional), and one for each concept. Each concept produces its own noise prediction — and what enters the sum is not that prediction itself, but its difference from the unconditional one: noise = uncond + v1×(noise_1 - uncond) + v2×(noise_2 - uncond) + ... Each v is that concept’s own guidance strength. A positive v pulls the image toward the concept (AND); a negative v pushes it away (NOT). Because every concept is scored separately at every step, none of them can be absorbed into another — which is exactly what happens inside a single fused prompt. The other place a run can combine the same concepts is the embedding: before the run their embeddings are interpolated into one. The direction turns from one concept towards the other, and the length runs between the lengths of the two readings. Only the ratio of the weights acts here, and with three or more concepts the order they stand in acts as well. The share the next concept gets is w2/(w1+w2), and only that ratio acts: multiplying every weight by -1 leaves the result bit for bit the same, so 1.00 and -2.00 give what -1.00 and 2.00 give. Weights of one sign put the share between 0 and 1, and the result between the concepts. Weights of different signs put it outside: 1.00 and -2.00 make the sum -1 and the share +2, 2.00 and -1.00 make it -1. Out there the result is no longer between the concepts. It turns past the one whose weight is the larger WITHOUT its sign, so the minus alone does not say which concept is left behind; single rows cross zero length and drop out while their neighbours are stretched. What a table like that paints is not read off the numbers. From there the run is the ordinary one, two passes per step: one for that one embedding, one for the negative prompt. The seed and the step count are the same for both places, so a pair of runs on one seed differs in the place.
technical.technical: Based on Liu et al. (2022), Eq. 11 (conjunction) and Eq. 15 (negation). Each concept is encoded with all three SD3.5 encoders (CLIP-L, OpenCLIP-G, T5-XXL) independently. The custom denoising loop calls pipe.transformer() once per concept per step. In the denoiser the weights are read in one of two ways. With "normalize" on, they are shares of the CFG value: the total guidance stays at CFG, so every concept you add makes each individual share smaller. With it off, each weight is that concept’s own guidance temperature, v = CFG × weight, and a negative weight is the NOT operator — algebraically identical to the paper’s eps_u + w×(eps_a - eps_b). A negative weight switches normalization off automatically, because a mixture with signs has no meaning. In the embedding neither reading applies: the concepts are interpolated there, so a weight acts through its ratio to the others, and with three or more concepts the order they stand in acts as well. VRAM: model weights are shared across passes; only activations vary. With 4 concepts, generation takes roughly 4x longer than standard (each step needs 5 transformer passes instead of 2).
technical.hints:
Instead of encoding your entire prompt as one monolithic vector, each concept gets its own transformer pass during denoising. Each one then adds its own pull on the image — or, with a negative weight, subtracts it.

A weight above 0 adds the concept (AND). A weight below 0 subtracts it (NOT) — which is not the same as putting it in the negative prompt. In the embedding only the RATIO of the weights acts: the share the next concept gets is w2/(w1+w2), and multiplying every weight by -1 changes nothing, so 1.00 and -2.00 give what -1.00 and 2.00 give. Two weights of one sign keep that share between 0 and 1 and the result between the concepts. Two weights of different signs send it outside, and the result then turns past the concept whose weight is larger without its sign.

Normalization is off while a concept is negated: a mixture with signs has no meaning, and each weight then acts as its own guidance strength in the denoiser (CFG × weight). It is off in the embedding as well: the run interpolates from one concept towards the next there, so a weight acts through its ratio to the others and there is nothing to normalize.

technical.brief: Representation Engineering, comparative model archaeology, and systematic bias analysis.
technical.hints: Representation Engineering, comparative model archaeology, and systematic bias analysis: Three research-based tools for investigating language models.

technical.what: Based on Zou et al. (2023), “Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency” (arXiv:2310.01405). While a language model writes, what it is about to say stands as a state of numbers, layer by layer. This instrument reads a direction out of that state — from a handful of sentence pairs somebody writes themselves — and adds that direction back into the state while the model writes. Nothing is trained: the reading and the steering both happen while the model runs. The method is Zou et al.’s reading vector alone: one direction over the whole hidden state, added to the output of one decoder layer. Li et al.’s Inference-Time Intervention (NeurIPS 2023) works differently — a probe per attention head, and a shift only on the heads that separate — which is why it left this surface’s reference list on 2026-08-24.
technical.how: What happens to the contrast pairs, in four steps. (1) Each pair is read twice: the model is given the upper sentence, then the lower one, and its inner state at the middle layer of the stack is taken at the last token of each. What the pair contributes is the difference between those two states. (2) What the pairs’ differences have in common is the direction. The drawing under the pairs shows it: one grey arrow per pair at the angle its difference has to that shared direction, and one green arrow for the shared direction itself — the one that goes into the writing. A wide fan means the pairs differ in several things and the reading keeps only what they share. (3) The direction is scaled to the distance the pairs themselves travel along it, so the strength counts in pair-differences: 1 adds exactly as much as one pair differs on average, and 2 pushes the state further than any of those sentence pairs ever stands from its own partner — which is why the text begins to break up above 2. The axis starts at 1.5, which tips the answer on the first press. (4) While the model writes, strength × direction is added to the output of that decoder layer, at every token, and the three columns show it pushed one way, left alone, and pushed the other way. WHY UNTRUE SENTENCES COME OUT: the next word is computed from that state alone, and every assertion the model makes comes from where the state stands. Move the state and you move what follows from it; whether what follows happens to be true is decided by where the state now stands, which is where the pairs put it. The instrument shows an assertion as a position, and a position can be shifted. WHY THE MIDDLE COLUMN SHOWS NOTHING: zero times the direction is the zero vector, so nothing at all is added there. That column is the run the model would have produced on its own, and it stands as the reference the other two are read against. English prompts work markedly better: most open-weight models were trained mostly on English.
technical.hints:
One axis, straight under the drawing, and it holds a distance from 0.5 to 3 with no sign: both directions run at every press and stand as the two outer columns (“against the arrow”, “no arrow”, “with the arrow”). It starts at 1.5, which tips the answer on the first press. The strength counts in pair-differences, so 1 is one pair’s worth of push; 0.5 to 2 is the usable band, and above 2 repetition and nonsense take over. In the middle column nothing is added at all — that is the model left alone, and it is there to read the other two against. Each press adds a row to the grid on the right: three cells from one reading and one seed, so two cells side by side differ in the push and in nothing else. The row keeps the prompt it was started with, and says once how hard it pushed and which layer it used.

Three pairs, editable, numbered, and each should differ in one thing. Three is also the ceiling: the button that adds one is gone at three. Once a run has been out, the pairs stand a second time as a drawing under the fields — one grey arrow per pair, each numbered, at the angle its difference has to the direction they share, and one green arrow for that shared direction, which is the one that goes into the writing. Arrows close together mean the pairs differ in the same thing; a wide fan means they differ in several, and the reading keeps only what they have in common. The arrangement is a PROJECTION and not a hand-drawn one: three differences stand at three angles to one another, and three rays from one point on a flat sheet have two free parameters, so a flat picture can hold two of the three angles at once. The plane drawn is the one the reading itself picks out — along the shared direction and across it — and the share of the spread that plane keeps comes back with every run. All arrows are drawn the same length, because a length here would say something about the drawing rather than about the pairs. The weights of the model stay as they are throughout: both the reading and the push happen while the model runs. Swapping a pair’s two sentences costs the measurement nothing — the direction is an eigenvector of a sum of outer products, and flipping one difference leaves its outer product as it was — it turns that one arrow around.

The layer is fixed at the middle of the stack and has no control on the surface. Depth decides what the same push changes: early layers still hold the words themselves, the last ones already hold the next word, and the middle is where a claim stands as a claim — so the middle is the one setting that produces something legible, and the others are settings that waste a run. It is taken from whatever model is chosen, so it follows the depth of that model’s stack; each row of results reports the number it used. An axis for it stood on the surface until 2026-08-25 and was removed.

goals.competence: Engage 3 — Evaluate whether AI outputs should be accepted, revised or rejected.
goals.expectation: Learners understand why AI-generated outputs should be verified and recognise how they can verify the content themselves.
goals.classroom: Learners review an AI-powered tool’s solution to a maths problem and accompanying explanation, then compare the AI-generated content to the process that their teacher has introduced to the class.
goals.how_de: Representation Engineering zeigt, warum Prüfen nötig ist: drei mitgelieferte Satzgruppen zu je drei Paaren („Fakten und ihre schlichten Gegenteile“, „Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four“, „Postfaktisch: Tatsache gegen Behauptung“) stellen je einen Satz gegen seine Umkehrung, und die Richtung aus einer Gruppe lässt sich beim Schreiben in das Modell zurückgeben. Was es dann schreibt, prüft die Gruppe an dem, was sie weiß; die Mathematikaufgabe der Maßnahme wird durch Sachsätze ersetzt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt das Modell einen kurzen Sachtext schreiben, einmal ohne und einmal mit der Richtung aus der Gruppe „Postfaktisch: Tatsache gegen Behauptung“, und unterstreicht in beiden Fassungen jede Behauptung, die sie selbst prüfen kann. Sie stellt fest, welche Fassung sich besser liest und welche stimmt.

technical.what: If an AI model carries prejudices, that can become unpleasant or even dangerous, because it often makes decisions, or prepares decisions — for example AI that is used by the police. On this page you can find out for yourselves whether language models carry prejudices. None of these questions is decidable, which is why “cannot be answered” is always the right answer. Still, the language models sometimes pick one of the other answers. Find out whether they then tend to pick the answer that matches the prejudice, or the other one. If a language model decides for the prejudice more often, its “bias score” under the graph goes up. The questions come from the “Bias Benchmark for QA dataset” (Parrish et al., Findings of ACL 2022; data CC BY 4.0 from github.com/nyu-mll/BBQ). Every run draws a fresh random sample of 60 out of the 2,836 open questions of that category.
technical.hints: The 2,836 above is the figure for Gender identity. Every category holds a different number of open questions — twice its situations: Age 1,840, Disability status 778, Nationality 1,540, Physical appearance 788, Race / ethnicity 3,440, Religion 600, Socio-economic status 3,432, Sexual orientation 432, Race x gender 7,980, Race x socio-economic status 5,580. The sample is always 60. Which of the three answers counts as the biased one is not decided by this platform: it comes with the data, per example, and it is polarity-specific — for one question the annotation points at the stereotyped group, for its counter-question at the other one. The bias score follows BBQ's own arithmetic and is scaled by how often the model named anyone at all, so 0 means nothing was measured, not that all is well. Under the score stands the median of every model series ever measured on this installation, from the second series on. At the kids safety level four of the eleven categories are offered — age, socio-economic status, nationality, disability — and within them the situations that turn on drugs, alcohol, violence, weapons, crime, terror, mental illness or sex are kept back, as whole situations and before the draw. The open questions a run can reach there are therefore fewer than the figures above: Age 1,124, Socio-economic status 2,868, Nationality 620, Disability status 382. Below the open level — at kids and at youth alike — six situations are kept back in every category: an autistic classmate mocked as weird, the ethnic body-odour trope, the submissive girlfriend or wife, being ranked by looks, same-sex marriage held against a religious conviction, and racism named as one of the two people's deed (858 of 14,623 situations, 5.9 %). Nothing is removed from the benchmark itself; the open level sees all of it.

goals.competence: Engage 6 — Explain how AI could be used to amplify societal biases.
goals.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
goals.classroom: Learners explore how and why facial recognition technology performs differently across demographics and discuss possible real-world impacts when it is used for decision making in everyday life.
goals.how_de: Bias Research 1 misst die Verzerrung eines Sprachmodells mit BBQ (Parrish u.a., Findings of ACL 2022): eine Lage, die offenlässt, wer gemeint ist, eine Frage, drei Antworten; für die gezeigten offenen Fragen ist „nicht beantwortbar“ die richtige Antwort. Wie oft ein Modell stattdessen jemanden nennt, und wen, steht als Kennzahl unter der Grafik; ein Lauf zeigt 60 offene Fragen der gewählten Kategorie und schickt dem Modell dazu die eindeutigen Gegenstücke als Kontrolle.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe wählt eine Kategorie (etwa Alter oder Nationalität), liest einige der 60 Fragen selbst und beantwortet sie, dann liest sie die Antworten des Modells und die Kennzahl. Sie bespricht, wen das Modell nennt, wenn nichts zu sagen wäre, und was das für Entscheidungen über Menschen heißt.

goals.competence: Shape 2 — Evaluate AI systems using defined criteria, expected outcomes, test cases and user feedback.
goals.expectation: Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests.
goals.classroom: Learners identify strategies they would use to solve a word puzzle. The teacher presents a sample algorithm for the same task. Using defined criteria (e.g. efficiency, consistency, clarity), learners compare their peers’ strategies to the algorithm, identifying strengths, limitations and trade-offs in each approach.
goals.how_de: Die Maßnahme vergleicht die Lösungsstrategien der Mitschülerinnen und Mitschüler für ein Worträtsel mit einem Algorithmus nach Kriterien (Effizienz, Konsistenz, Klarheit). Bias Research 1 ist der Benchmark-Fall dafür: BBQ-Fragen mit festgelegtem Sollwert (für die gezeigten offenen Fragen ist „nicht beantwortbar“ die richtige Antwort), die Kennzahl des Modells unter der Grafik. Die Gruppe kann dieselben Fragen selbst beantworten und sich mit dem Modell vergleichen.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe beantwortet zwanzig der gestellten Fragen selbst, dann liest sie die Antworten des Modells und die Kennzahl. Sie vergleicht nach Konsistenz (wer bleibt bei „nicht beantwortbar“?) und bespricht, was der Maßstab misst und was nicht.

Learners develop better descriptions using technically accurate and age-appropriate language, then reflect on how language shapes their understanding of what AI can or cannot do.
goals.how_de: Für die Redeweise „die KI versteht“ liefert Bias Research 2 den Prüffall: 60 Satzpaare je Lauf aus WinoBias (Zhao u.a., NAACL 2018), die sich in einem Wort unterscheiden und bei denen der Bezug annotiert und in beiden derselbe ist; die Grafik zählt, wie oft die Antwort des Modells mit dem Pronomen kippt.
goals.practice_de: Die Gruppe lässt einen Lauf über die 60 Paare gehen und liest in der Grafik ab, wie oft die Antwort kippt. Dann prüft sie den Satz „die KI versteht den Satz“ an dem, was sie gezählt hat, und schreibt eine Beschreibung, die ohne „verstehen“ auskommt.
